title: Scott Jenson on Evolving Desktop OS, Local-First, & Agentic UX

>> [music]
>> Hello everybody. I'm Olimpiu Pop, an
InfoQ editor, and today I have in front
of me Scott Jensen.
For those of you with the name doesn't
say nothing, he's probably one of the UX
designers that has
a lot of impact on your life or the
things that you're doing if you're using
a MacBook or you're if you're using an
Android phone,
because he worked on a lot of this
stuff.
Thank you, Scott, for talking to us.
>> Great, I'm happy to be here. Yeah, I
basically started off at Apple. I worked
on the Macintosh
System 7. Um I then worked over and
moved over to the the Newton, which was
a a big handheld at the time, got a lot
of hype, then moved over to do a lot of
desktop work. I ended up working at
Google and worked on the first version
of Google Mobile Maps, went over and
worked on the Chrome team, had a project
called the Physical Web, and then did
quite a bit of consulting. I was at Frog
Design for a number of years as creative
director and worked on some big projects
for say HP and and uh Disney.
And went back to Google at the end of my
career, but 2 years ago I left Google.
I'm now kind of working on my own.
>> I liked one of your talks and the way
how you framed the current work that
that you're doing. You mentioned that
you're repenting for your sins in the
last period, and that's why a lot of
your work is currently in open source.
Thank you for taking the energy and time
during this period and doing that much
exploration, and that's why we are
together because
you did have, I think, almost a year
ago, it was an at Ubuntu, I think,
conference where you spoke about the
past, present, and future maybe, but
more on the present and future of what
UX for desktop means.
That got a lot of traction. I think it
was last time when I checked it was half
a million views, and then I saw the
presentation that you had at Local
First, not that much traction because
it's more current than the other one,
but what you had different there, you
had a couple of ideas that you shared.
Actually, you put your fingers or your
ideas, creative ideas, into practice,
and you provided a couple of ideas how
UX can look for desktop and to better
organize your work. But, let's not get
ahead of ourselves and take a step back.
Let's look a little bit, as you
mentioned,
you grew through the phases of what
desktop means.
Let's look at how the UX
in the desktop space evolved, and maybe
touch a bit, if you think it's useful,
on the differences between
mobile and desktop, because even though
mobile is around with us for some time
now,
we are still using desktop, and
there is no sense of something that will
come and replace them. That people tried
to replace them with the tablets, but
that's nowhere near into into that term.
>> Well, I think you you covered a lot of
the kind of the the key hits I've been
talking about over the last couple
years. The first one is just that the
desktop has basically stopped evolving
like for the last 20 years.
Apple [snorts] has introduced 12-ish
features in the last, say, 15 years, but
they're all about making the ecosystem
better, you know, universal clipboard or
the phone being used on the desktop or
AirDrop or things like that. So, the
vast majority of the improvement with a
Macintosh has been to tighten its
control around its ecosystem, and the
desktop itself has not fundamentally
changed. And that transitions to what
you were just mentioning about mobile,
that a lot of people feel like all the
hotness, all the excitement is in
mobile. But the point I made in my talk
is that mobile won consumers, right? It
didn't win productivity. So, back around
2015, all these companies tried multiple
companies. At Google, they tried this,
they called it tablet Tuesdays. And they
was like, "Everybody bring a tablet to
work and do all of your work on a
tablet." And that was a disaster.
It's not that tablets are bad, it's just
that tablets are hyper-focused on things
like content and gaming and you know,
social media. And so, mobile and tablets
are very good at a very narrow set of
things. And so, a lot of my work has
been trying to say,
"Let's not throw desktop out. What is it
about desktop that is so powerful? And
then how can we inject some of that into
mobile?" It's not either or, it's about
what's good. And so,
I've wanted to both improve mobile, but
in the talk I gave at Ubuntu was I also
wanted to improve desktop.
And my general thesis is that we don't
seem to be that excited about improving
things. We just kind of accept the
status quo. And I gave a couple of ideas
on that.
>> This thing what you're saying, yes, we
have tablet and it's useful for some
stuff. We have mobile and it's useful
for some stuff.
But desktop is still king in a couple of
categories and that's very useful.
That sounds a lot like cloud where you
have everything across the board and
then you regardless of what you're
using, you'll have those things.
But given that now our discussion
started around local first and
what that tries, I had a similar
conversation with Adam Wiggins which is
involved both with local first, but he
also was one of the pioneers of the
cloud with Heroku and bringing things
between developers. And one of the
conclusions of our conversation at that
point was we have a tendency as
technologists to go
from one extreme to the other. We moved
from desktop,
we moved all the way to the cloud
and now we are realizing that
that abstraction is
too much and we miss some of the points
and now we have to find a sweet spot and
that doesn't have to be something set in
stone but it will be probably something
like uh
gradient. You're moving left and right
depending on what's the scenario or
different types of approaches.
What's your take on it? How do you feel
about it? What will be the things that
we can take from I don't know, maybe
mobile, maybe desktop and what will be
the points that we need?
>> Again, you touched on many points there.
I think the big issue with the cloud
Well, there's there's lots of things to
talk about but the the two big ones is
privacy.
The idea is that with a cloud
all of your data is with one particular
provider and so this is a well-known
issue people talked about I'm not the
first one to mention this and that's why
local first gets a little bit worried
that you're giving all your data to
Google or all your data to Microsoft.
And so there's that aspect of it but the
other one is just simply pragmatic which
is to say
we live in a world where you don't
always have connectivity, right? And so
how do you continue to work on something
if it's in the cloud because you're cut
off and whenever there's an AWS outage
the world seems to always rediscover
this fragility of it. And so there's a
both a practical and a philosophical
reason I think for talking about it. But
like you said, we don't want to throw
the baby out with the bathwater. It's
not like cloud is inherently wrong. I
think local first is just trying to
build it so it's
robust. So I can keep all of my data,
you can't take it away from me and if
the cloud goes away I can continue to
work on it. And that feels like a very
powerful thing that cuts through all of
local first.
>> Yeah, and I think it's uh well, it's
more heavyweight than what we're
discussing but distribution of of load
is something quite important and that
goes around in pretty much all aspects
of technology in life. I'm I'm just
thinking now I'm based in Romania, so
that means that we have a
a huge neighboring country called
Ukraine that has a problem for the last
couple of years, and that means that if
the things are not distributed, they
have a huge problem with bombardment
just taking out electricity. And I think
that's something important also for us.
Just distributing stuff, as you
mentioned,
across we have different copies,
and there are other problems to that,
but that's a whole different
conversation, as you mentioned.
So, now we have more or less two
different trends, if you want. We have
the Linux-based family of systems, and I
think you know about all the open-source
distributions,
or the ones that got forked from them,
more or less, like macOS back in its
infancy, and then we have Windows.
What do you think? Where does the
creativity coming from? Because they
have a tendency of copying each other.
It's just uh like a game of tag.
Where is the creativity coming from at
this point?
>> Yeah, that's an interesting question
because
as a UX designer, what I would say was
that Apple
was always trying to kind of, initially,
just really solve deeper problems. Where
did he I worked at Apple for a number
for eight years, and it was just like,
what did people need, right? And what do
we want to do? And
I think all tech companies have changed
recently. So, I don't want to single out
any one particular one, but Apple and
frankly Google have been what do we
need, right? It's that's it's why I felt
like I had to leave Google. It was all
about the money.
And when I was at Google, we really were
a bunch of boy scouts, and we just
wanted to do what was right, and the
money would follow. It's not like we
didn't want money. It was just more
like, if we did the right thing, it
would take care of itself. And it's
become so clearly about lock-in. I mean,
what Google has done with Android and
Chrome, and what Apple has done with
Safari and locking out browsers. This is
not for users. This is not a user
empowerment strategy. This is locking
you into our ecosystem so we get our 15%
of the revenue.
And so yeah, I think there's a natural
frustration with us, for lack of a
better word, late stage capitalism that
is showing up in these companies and
I refuse this framing like, well, you
got to eat somehow, which just gives up
any attempt at ethics or longer term
thinking. And
I believe that there is a win-win here.
You know, you can make money and you can
think longer term. And in fact, as a UX
designer, you're frequently making this
play to companies, which is to say, yes,
if we do this UX work, it's going to
cost a little bit more money, but you're
going to get brand loyalty, you're going
to get less errors, you're going to have
less callbacks. So
this idea about investing in the future
to get bigger returns
is kind of at the heart of social
democracy. It's it's a it's a longer
term vision that means that we can do
the right thing and possibly make money.
>> Yeah, I I agree with you and while
listening to you, an idea was just
spinning in my head.
>> [gasps]
>> It's all nice and cozy thinking about
having partially the data that you
normally need in your pocket, on your
phone or tablet or whatever.
But the tendency of the standards and I
know that it's that's a topic that you
touched upon
is that the images, for instance,
they're are so huge
and once you put them on iCloud
they have a tendency of providing very
small thumbnails on your phone, but you
still need the cloud.
So even though I have a
what I consider something that is very
generous, it's a 250 gigabytes of memory
of space on my phone, it's always full
and whenever I want to check up a photo,
it's like, "Okay, your connectivity is
not that great. So, please
rejoin the Wi-Fi." So, I think that's
one of the challenges into probably a
degrading way of looking at it. I
remember back in the day, 10 years ago,
we developed an application, and we had
a degrading level of quality. For
instance, if uh
I was on my mobile phone, the photo was
up to a given resolution. And then, if I
was on a more powerful device like a
tablet or even a a MacBook, I was
providing different degrees. And then,
that allowed us to zoom in or zoom out,
depending on the resources that we had.
And as you mentioned, there is an
ecosystem where everybody tries to lock
you in, and I do have to admit that the
Apple ecosystem is very well integrated.
Everybody else is
years light-years away.
>> Yeah.
>> But, that's my problem, as you
mentioned.
If I need or a very simple scenario, for
me it happens that I need to send emails
from my mobile phone. I download
something, and I cannot find the file
anymore.
>> Right.
>> And then, it's a lot easier to just
go to my MacBook. But, I think these are
the points that you had as well, and
going back to desktop, what's the
the real problem, or how you call it,
the curse of direct manipulation? I
think you you referred to it. What are
the building blocks that you we are
starting when we're looking at desktop?
>> Yeah. Well, the previous point you made
about the downloading a file and then
not being able to find it on your phone,
that is a a fundamental problem of
mobile, because what mobile did was it
hid effectively files within each
application.
So, if I want to edit a file in another
application on mobile, it's nearly
impossible. Right. The only way I can do
it is to share it to the other
application, which often makes a copy,
and there is a file manager, but most
apps don't use it. In fact, I have a
whole blog series about this and how we
can have the best of both worlds. We can
have the simplicity of hiding files
uh within applications, but we can
expose them as files. That's a a
separate conversation about just
evolving the mobile system to be more
file-friendly, but keeping this whole
self-contained model that makes them so
much simpler.
But now, going back to your cursor
direct manipulation, I I used that kind
of with my LNK quote, that perspective
is worth 20, you know, 80 IQ points.
And so, by understanding a little bit
more about what the desktop has
historically done, it gave us
perspective to figure out what we want
to do to improve it. And so, the idea
there was that direct manipulation is
stateless. You cut, you paste, you type,
you open, you close, and they're all
these atomic elements that let you
manipulate a document. It's It's all
good, no one's complaining, but it's by
design stateless. It doesn't remember
what you did, it has no history of what
you've done.
And so, I used that as my perspective to
say, "What would happen if we had an
operating system that actually
remembered a little bit more of what you
did?" And then I had three different
prototypes that kind of showed, you
know, what that was like. Because that
would allow effectively a little bit
more
stuff to happen and gives us support.
Because to me, the whole purpose of an
operating system is to support the user
doing work.
And direct manipulation is one level of
support, but then the next one is this
ability to help me maintain my context,
so I can come back from lunch and I can
keep working.
>> Yeah, so taking a step back, it's
something that
just circled in different environments.
People are saying, "Okay, data is the
new oil and stuff like that." So, that's
kind of true also for us, because in the
end, if you get a laptop and it doesn't
have anything on it, it's just a machine
that is very powerful, but doesn't have
the ability. Once you have an operating
system on it, you have a collection of
applications that allow you to do basic
stuff. But once you start using it for
you,
you have files and all those aggregated.
But
if you'll open the downloads folder for
instance, that's crazy. It it will be
impossible. And what you you mentioned
and what you underline now as well is
it should be an extension of ourself,
our brains, and have also a working
memory, some kind of metadata that will
allow you more or more context. And the
isn't is the facility through which we
are mentioning to do that,
it will allow you to make things a lot
easier and then just resume at different
points and then avoid the different
types of
system of
that you need to just do by hand.
>> Yeah, exactly.
>> You had also a couple of suggestions.
You didn't just put the finger on the
wound, but you had a couple of
proposals. Three of them if I remember
correctly.
What do you think this point would make
our lives as users of desktop easier?
What would be the options that we have
on the table?
>> Well, yeah, I I have a whole talk I can
give on that one if you want. But no,
the
No, no, no, no, but the the the three
prototypes that I showed at the Local
First conference was about this idea of
effectively working memory. The first
one was about trying to not be blinkered
by the small screens on mobile or
frankly even laptops. And so, imagine we
had a bigger screen and what could we do
with that? And so, I had effectively a
window manager that allowed you to
spread things out so that you had a a
wide range. And that gets into human
perception and how it's very easy for
the human eye to kind of look left and
right on the horizon and see things in
the distance. And so, the idea was to
have all of the activity that you're
doing kind of spread out in a very
helpful way that gives you the ability
to find things quickly.
I have a lot of issues with people in
the Linux community because they are
very smart
and they're very organized, and that
creates a certain type of very rigid
software. Uh and the example I gave is
virtual desktops. Virtual desktops are
very powerful, but they only really work
if you're really smart and really
organized. And I think a lot of the
world is very organic and messy. We all
have desktops where things are piled on
it. And so I kind of wanted to have a
windowing system that was kind of the
anti-Linux approach, which was just more
organic. So that was the first one was a
window manager that kind of spread
everything out. But the other one was to
say that we've all been in the situation
where you cut and paste something and
it's lost because you cut something else
on top of it. And yes, all operating
systems now have a clipboard history,
but we don't really use it. They're kind
of a pain. It's like, "Oh, it's the
seventh thing down." Or, you know, you
could in theory go into one field and
cut every single field out and go to
another field and paste them all back in
again but
that's nearly impossible. It's tedious.
It's just so hard to get. So the idea
was to say, "How could we elevate this
whole copy-paste
history model?" So I created a system
where, a little bit like Obsidian, we
had a little side drawer, and you could
put all of your clipboard history in
there or the files that you're working
on or sub things. It was meant to be
effectively a little mini context window
that allowed you to kind of store all
your data for that particular project.
And you could open and close it like a
file, but it acted like a folder. And so
it was meant to be a way for you to have
working memory of that stuff. And then
the final one was more of a history that
was totally stolen from a classic paper
in the '90s called Lifestreams.
And the idea was to say, "Well, what
have I've been doing the whole day? Just
give me a ribbon of everything I've been
doing, but provide some clever
visualizations."
Because once you give someone some
scaffolding, a memory scaffolding, it's
like, "Oh, right. That's what I did
right before I talked to the computer.
This is what I did before lunch. This is
what I did." And it gives you a a little
bit of a structure, and you can find
things effectively by adjacency.
And so, these aren't the only three
things that we could be talking about,
but it is an attempt at me to articulate
and give examples of how we can have an
operating system go well beyond what
it's been doing today. And I hope it got
people excited.
>> Okay. So, we are looking about the
working
memory and how the things are being done
and different perspectives on top of
that. One of them, as you mentioned, was
spatial, and that allows you to organize
it in a different way, but not in the
way with virtual desktops we have
because my feeling is that the always
when I'm looking at virtual desktops, it
feels that I have, you know, my my ski
suit on, and I have so many pockets, but
I I it seems that I'm I'm not ever able
to find the car keys or anything else,
especially when I'm wearing the the ski
gloves. That's one, and then that allows
you one important aspect that for me it
was really impressive was the fact that
even the the smaller files are useful.
So, meaning that you can see the data
there, and you can just use them. For
instance, you had the example of a music
player, and then that depending on the
way how it's zooming in or zooming out,
it just changes shape, and it's it's
still useful. The other one is in terms
of a timeline of what we actually
worked, and then allows you to look at
the things differently,
or the clipboard being organized in a
associative manner where you have
different things that are grouped in the
way that it's better.
What do you think are the things that
would be useful just as guidelines, like
best practices? You mentioned you have
more, so if there is anything that needs
to be
brought to light?
>> Well, my overall thesis is the desktop,
and frankly mobile,
have gotten frozen in time.
And all I want us to do
is to try a little harder, you know, to
just explore a little bit. So, I've
written on my blog, I have the future of
files and the present of files that
talks of how we can extend mobile. I've
done work in the past with Google. I did
a project called eloquent, which is also
on my blog, that talks about how we
could significantly improve text editing
on mobile. And then of course these
three concepts I just did on the
desktop. So, all I want us to do, my my
my primary goal here is to say there's
so much we could be exploring and the
world is not set in stone. But so often
people think that I want to blow
everything up and and there's a crowd of
people that says it's taken us 30 years
to get to this point. Don't blow it up.
And I'm like, "Well, I don't want to
blow it up." I mean, things are always
changing and we're not going to use the
same desktop 50 years from now.
Something's going to change and right
now the way things are looking is we're
just going to let Apple hand us the keys
to the future because they're going to
define what we want to do. And they
clearly aren't earning that right. And
frankly neither is Google. Now, I know
I'm becoming a little little bit more of
a radical here, but I mean my point is
to say let's appreciate that there's
more to do. And so, I gave you three
examples. I know there's a gazillion
more. And so, I don't have anything
specific other than those three.
But what I am doing is I'm actually
trying to turn my prototypes into real
code. Because that also helps. So, the
last one I gave you the the live
streams, that shows me I've now got it
written as a Chrome extension and as a
Swift extension and it's capturing
desktop events and it's capturing Chrome
events and it's putting it together into
a single thing. And I'm going to be
giving another talk in September at KDE
and I'm hoping to have it done in time
for that. And then I'll open source
that, of course, so everyone can play
with it. But it raises, by the way, all
sorts of privacy issues. But the goal
right now is to just try and to see if
it's powerful and if it's helpful. And
then if it is, then we have to then
have further conversations because
there is this tension between a system
that remembers and does things for you
is also a privacy risk. How do you
navigate that and how do you make sure
that that's done in a way that's
protective of the user? And so there's a
deeper conversation to have there.
>> So we're looking forward to your work.
Good luck with getting it in time for in
September. There is not that much time
until then. So best of luck with that.
And I'll try to add another point based
also on the conversations we had and
also on your talks.
And that's standards.
Because now there are a couple of
ecosystems and I'm just thinking now
about Apple. I would have stayed away
from that. But you did mention earlier
AirDrop. And my feeling is that AirDrop
is such a great technology, especially
when you have people in the proximity
and you don't want to go all the way
through the cloud and send them on
different type of messaging apps. But
that works only in the Apple ecosystem.
>> That recently changed, right? And now
Android basically has figured that out
and so that works.
>> And that's where I wanted to get to is
the fact that there is a lot of effort
on the European Union side to just open
that up, to create a standard based on
it. AirDrop started it.
And it seems that the point regulation
is useful as well. Do you think
standards are is also an important
aspect to just have this bridge across
different technology gaps? Is it
something to worth to keep in mind?
>> Oh, absolutely. But I mean, whenever you
say the word standards, every tech bro
in the room will stand up and yell,
"You're killing creativity." You know,
and then you can And so I want to make
sure we acknowledge this is a
challenging issue. But like, say for
example, getting Apple to get rid of the
lightning connector to go to USB-C.
That would have never happened if it
hadn't been for the EU. And so that was
I think very good pressure. And again,
it shows the fact that from an e-waste
point of view, it's the right thing to
do to have one universal connector,
but it was not in Apple's best interest.
It was in the world's best interest.
I wouldn't call that a standards
conversation. I would just call that
kind of a compliance conversation.
>> Yep. Yep.
>> And so I do think that there is a bigger
role for governments to force companies
to think longer term. And I'm going to
go back to my radical roots here about
late-stage capitalism. It's not that
these companies are necessarily evil as
much as people like to say they are. I
like to say that they are amoral.
They're not immoral. They just
don't care. They literally only care
about this very, very short-term
effects, which is why we have global
warming and and other things as well. So
to me, the way of framing it is what's
the longer-term goal because there's
money involved. It costs money to think
longer term. And so how do we do that in
a way that is fair to these companies,
but frankly is also fair to us? And
because I think the vast majority of the
decision-making has been only what's
fair to the companies, it's been
extremely one-sided. So I do believe
it's time for a little bit of pushback.
>> I would normally refrain from having
these kind of comments, especially in a
time-bounded context, but you mentioned
radical twice already, so I have to
mention my radical perspective as well.
You're totally right that companies tend
to look only at their interest, but that
interest is fueled by our comfort
because we have a tendency, and you can
see that all across as humans we have
Okay, it's a lot easier to
bookmark a page, but rather than
bookmarking it and being organized, and
that gets us to the initial point. We
use Google search engine.
And that's obviously something that goes
all across the internet.
It's
burning fuel and so on and so forth. And
now with LLMs, that's even more so.
>> Agreed.
>> Ethical aspects, environmental aspects,
and so on and so forth. So, if we would
be more
concerned about the future because the
general population will be the most
affected by climate change and all the
other problems,
the companies will have to stand up to
their standards and you can see those
points mainly across the last couple of
months
when there is this sovereignty movement
in Europe and where we just realized
that we do have things as well.
And I'm happy to see that we still have
people that are aligned across the pound
in terms of what are the European, the
Western values, and what do you think to
just make sure that greed is not only
thing that is fueling technology and
everything else.
>> No, I completely agree. And there's
multiple forces involved. So, we talked
just ago we talked about the role of
governments to kind of force these
things, but also there's the role of
technology, right? Like for example,
what's going on right now with LLMs and
the big data centers and so forth.
There is likely going to be a
technological force that's outside of
the governments, which is to say we're
going to over the next 5 years
have machines that are significantly
more powerful and we're going to have
open-source local models that can run
locally. And this mirrors what's
happened throughout the history of
technology, whether you're
